nodes.name: Prime Number
nodes.statement: A natural number p >= 2 whose only divisors are 1 and p.

nodes.name: Greatest Common Divisor
nodes.statement: gcd(a,b) is the largest natural number dividing both a and b.

nodes.name: Coprime Integers
nodes.statement: a and b are coprime if gcd(a,b) = 1.

nodes.name: Modular Congruence
nodes.statement: a ≡ b (mod n) iff n divides a - b.

nodes.name: Ring ZMod n
nodes.statement: ZMod n is the ring of integers modulo n.

nodes.name: Euler's Totient Function
nodes.statement: phi(n) counts integers 1 <= k <= n coprime to n.

nodes.name: Legendre Symbol
nodes.statement: (a/p) = 1 if a is a QR mod p, -1 if not, 0 if p | a.

nodes.name: Moebius Function
nodes.statement: mu(n) = (-1)^k if n is product of k distinct primes, 0 if n has squared prime factor.

nodes.name: p-adic Valuation
nodes.statement: v_p(n) is the largest power of prime p dividing n.

nodes.name: Primitive Root
nodes.statement: g is a primitive root mod n if its multiplicative order equals phi(n).

nodes.name: Fermat's Little Theorem
nodes.statement: If p is prime and gcd(a,p) = 1, then a^{p-1} ≡ 1 (mod p).

nodes.name: Euler's Theorem
nodes.statement: If gcd(a,n) = 1 then a^{phi(n)} ≡ 1 (mod n).

nodes.name: Wilson's Theorem
nodes.statement: p >= 2 is prime iff (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p).

nodes.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem
nodes.statement: If gcd(m,n) = 1 then ZMod(mn) ≅ ZMod(m) × ZMod(n).

nodes.name: Quadratic Reciprocity
nodes.statement: For odd primes p,q: (p/q)(q/p) = (-1)^{(p-1)/2·(q-1)/2}.

nodes.name: Bezout's Identity
nodes.statement: For a,b ∈ Z, there exist x,y with ax + by = gcd(a,b).

nodes.name: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
nodes.statement: Every integer > 1 has a unique prime factorization.

nodes.name: Infinitude of Primes
nodes.statement: There are infinitely many prime numbers.

nodes.name: Euclid's Lemma
nodes.statement: If prime p divides ab, then p divides a or p divides b.

nodes.name: Bertrand's Postulate
nodes.statement: For every n >= 1, there exists a prime p with n < p <= 2n.

nodes.name: Dirichlet's Theorem on Primes in APs
nodes.statement: For coprime a,d, there are infinitely many primes ≡ a (mod d).

nodes.name: Sum of Two Squares
nodes.statement: Odd prime p = a² + b² iff p ≡ 1 (mod 4).

nodes.name: Lagrange's Four Squares Theorem
nodes.statement: Every positive integer is the sum of four squares.

nodes.name: Sum of Totient over Divisors
nodes.statement: Σ_{d|n} phi(d) = n for all n >= 1.

nodes.name: Chevalley-Warning Theorem
nodes.statement: If polynomials over F_p have total degree < number of variables, p divides the number of common zeros.

nodes.name: Hensel's Lemma
nodes.statement: A simple root mod p lifts uniquely to Z_p.

nodes.name: QR Second Supplement
nodes.statement: (2/p) = (-1)^{(p²-1)/8}: 2 is a QR mod p iff p ≡ ±1 (mod 8).

nodes.name: Lucas' Theorem
nodes.statement: C(m,n) ≡ Π C(m_i,n_i) (mod p) where m_i,n_i are base-p digits.

nodes.name: Legendre's Formula
nodes.statement: v_p(n!) = Σ_{i≥1} floor(n/p^i).

nodes.name: Freshman's Dream
nodes.statement: In characteristic p: (a + b)^p = a^p + b^p.

nodes.name: Finite Field Multiplicative Group is Cyclic
nodes.statement: The multiplicative group of any finite field is cyclic.

nodes.name: Square Root of 2 is Irrational
nodes.statement: √2 is not rational.

nodes.name: Pi is Irrational
nodes.statement: π is irrational.

nodes.name: Lifting the Exponent Lemma
nodes.statement: For odd prime p with p | a-b, p ∤ a: v_p(aⁿ - bⁿ) = v_p(a-b) + v_p(n).

nodes.name: Order Divides Group Order
nodes.statement: In a finite group, ord(g) divides |G|.

nodes.name: Finite Set (Finset)
nodes.statement: A finite set with decidable membership and cardinality.

nodes.name: Binomial Coefficient
nodes.statement: C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n-k)!) counts k-element subsets of [n].

nodes.name: Simple Graph
nodes.statement: G = (V,E) with irreflexive symmetric edge relation.

nodes.name: Chromatic Number
nodes.statement: χ(G) is the minimum colors for a proper vertex coloring.

nodes.name: Antichain
nodes.statement: A set of pairwise incomparable elements in a poset.

nodes.name: Partition of n
nodes.statement: A multiset of positive integers summing to n.

nodes.name: Catalan Numbers
nodes.statement: C_n = C(2n,n)/(n+1) counts binary trees, Dyck paths, etc.

nodes.name: Matroid
nodes.statement: A combinatorial structure generalizing linear independence.

nodes.name: Graph Matching
nodes.statement: A set of pairwise non-adjacent edges.

nodes.name: Graph Connectivity
nodes.statement: G is connected if every two vertices are joined by a path.

nodes.name: Pigeonhole Principle
nodes.statement: If n+1 objects go in n boxes, some box has ≥ 2.

nodes.name: Binomial Theorem
nodes.statement: (x+y)^n = Σ C(n,k) x^{n-k} y^k.

nodes.name: Sperner's Theorem
nodes.statement: Max antichain in P([n]) has size C(n, ⌊n/2⌋).

nodes.name: Erdos-Ko-Rado Theorem
nodes.statement: Max intersecting k-uniform family of [n] (n≥2k) has size C(n-1,k-1).

nodes.name: Turan's Theorem
nodes.statement: Max edges in K_{r+1}-free graph on n vertices is (1-1/r)n²/2.

nodes.name: Handshaking Lemma
nodes.statement: Sum of degrees = 2 × number of edges.

nodes.name: Kruskal-Katona Theorem
nodes.statement: Initial segments in colex minimize shadow size among k-uniform families of given size.

nodes.name: Vandermonde's Identity
nodes.statement: C(m+n,r) = Σ_{k=0}^r C(m,k)C(n,r-k).

nodes.name: Zorn's Lemma
nodes.statement: If every chain in a poset has an upper bound, there exists a maximal element.

nodes.name: Binomial Symmetry
nodes.statement: C(n,k) = C(n,n-k).

nodes.name: Polynomial Ring
nodes.statement: R[X] is the ring of polynomials with coefficients in R.

nodes.name: Complex Numbers
nodes.statement: ℂ = ℝ × ℝ with multiplication (a,b)(c,d) = (ac-bd, ad+bc).

nodes.name: Inner Product Space
nodes.statement: A vector space with a positive-definite Hermitian form ⟨·,·⟩.

nodes.name: Norm
nodes.statement: A function ‖·‖ satisfying positivity, homogeneity, triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Algebraic Closure
nodes.statement: An algebraically closed field extension in which every polynomial splits.

nodes.name: Absolute Value
nodes.statement: |x| = x if x ≥ 0, -x if x < 0.

nodes.name: Root of Polynomial
nodes.statement: r is a root of f if f(r) = 0.

nodes.name: Degree of Polynomial
nodes.statement: deg(f) is the highest power with nonzero coefficient.

nodes.name: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
nodes.statement: Every non-constant polynomial over ℂ has a root in ℂ.

nodes.name: AM-GM Inequality
nodes.statement: For non-negative reals: (a₁+...+aₙ)/n ≥ (a₁·...·aₙ)^{1/n}.

nodes.name: Triangle Inequality
nodes.statement: ‖a + b‖ ≤ ‖a‖ + ‖b‖ in any normed space.

nodes.name: Factor Theorem
nodes.statement: r is a root of f iff (x-r) divides f.

nodes.name: Power Mean Inequality
nodes.statement: M_r(x) ≤ M_s(x) for r ≤ s, where M_r is the r-th power mean.

nodes.name: Hilbert Basis Theorem
nodes.statement: If R is Noetherian, then R[X] is Noetherian.

nodes.name: Polynomial GCD Exists
nodes.statement: k[X] is a Euclidean domain, so GCDs exist.

nodes.name: Continuous Function
nodes.statement: f is continuous at a if lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a).

nodes.name: Differentiable Function
nodes.statement: f is differentiable at a if the limit (f(a+h)-f(a))/h exists.

nodes.name: Riemann Integral
nodes.statement: ∫_a^b f(x)dx as limit of Riemann sums.

nodes.name: Compact Set
nodes.statement: A set is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover.

nodes.name: Sequence Convergence
nodes.statement: aₙ → L if for every ε > 0, |aₙ - L| < ε for sufficiently large n.

nodes.name: Series Convergence
nodes.statement: Σ aₙ converges if its partial sums converge.

nodes.name: Metric Space
nodes.statement: A set with a distance function d satisfying positivity, symmetry, triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Measure
nodes.statement: A countably additive set function μ: Σ → [0,∞].

nodes.name: Mean Value Theorem
nodes.statement: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), ∃c: f'(c) = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a).

nodes.name: Intermediate Value Theorem
nodes.statement: A continuous function on [a,b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b).

nodes.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 1)
nodes.statement: If F' = f (continuous), then ∫_a^b f(x)dx = F(b) - F(a).

nodes.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 2)
nodes.statement: d/dx ∫_a^x f(t)dt = f(x) for continuous f.

nodes.name: Rolle's Theorem
nodes.statement: If f(a) = f(b) and f is differentiable on (a,b), ∃c: f'(c) = 0.

nodes.name: Extreme Value Theorem
nodes.statement: A continuous function on a compact set attains its max and min.

nodes.name: Monotone Convergence Theorem
nodes.statement: If fₙ ↑ f pointwise (non-negative measurable), then ∫fₙ → ∫f.

nodes.name: Dominated Convergence Theorem
nodes.statement: If fₙ → f a.e. and |fₙ| ≤ g (integrable), then ∫fₙ → ∫f.

nodes.name: Squeeze Theorem
nodes.statement: If aₙ ≤ bₙ ≤ cₙ and aₙ,cₙ → L, then bₙ → L.

nodes.name: Comparison Test for Series
nodes.statement: If 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ and Σbₙ converges, then Σaₙ converges.

nodes.name: Ratio Test
nodes.statement: If |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| → L < 1, then Σaₙ converges absolutely.

nodes.name: Stone-Weierstrass Theorem
nodes.statement: A subalgebra of C(X,ℝ) separating points is dense in C(X,ℝ).

nodes.name: Inverse Function Theorem
nodes.statement: If f'(a) is invertible, then f is a local diffeomorphism near a.

nodes.name: Implicit Function Theorem
nodes.statement: If F(a,b)=0 and ∂F/∂y is invertible at (a,b), there exists g with F(x,g(x))=0 near a.

nodes.name: Heine-Borel Theorem
nodes.statement: In ℝⁿ, a set is compact iff closed and bounded.

nodes.name: Banach Fixed Point Theorem
nodes.statement: A contraction on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point.

nodes.name: Angle Between Vectors
nodes.statement: The angle θ with cos θ = ⟨u,v⟩/(‖u‖·‖v‖).

nodes.name: Convex Set
nodes.statement: S is convex if for x,y ∈ S and t ∈ [0,1]: tx + (1-t)y ∈ S.

nodes.name: Triangle
nodes.statement: Three non-collinear points in an affine space.

nodes.name: Pythagorean Theorem
nodes.statement: In a right triangle: a² + b² = c².

nodes.name: Law of Cosines
nodes.statement: c² = a² + b² - 2ab·cos(C).

nodes.name: Triangle Inequality
nodes.statement: d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y) + d(y,z) in any metric space.

nodes.name: Riesz Representation (Hilbert)
nodes.statement: Every continuous linear functional on a Hilbert space is ⟨·,y⟩ for unique y.

nodes.name: Vector Space
nodes.statement: A module over a field.

nodes.name: Linear Map
nodes.statement: f(αu + βv) = αf(u) + βf(v).

nodes.name: Matrix
nodes.statement: An m × n array of elements from a ring.

nodes.name: Determinant
nodes.statement: det(A) = Σ_{σ∈Sₙ} sgn(σ) Π aᵢ,σ(ᵢ).

nodes.name: Rank
nodes.statement: rank(f) = dim(image(f)) for a linear map f.

nodes.name: Rank-Nullity Theorem
nodes.statement: dim(V) = rank(f) + nullity(f) for linear f: V → W.

nodes.name: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
nodes.statement: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial.

nodes.name: Determinant is Multiplicative
nodes.statement: det(AB) = det(A)·det(B).

nodes.name: Cramer's Rule
nodes.statement: xᵢ = det(Aᵢ)/det(A) where Aᵢ replaces column i with b.

nodes.name: Every Vector Space Has a Basis
nodes.statement: Every vector space (over a division ring) has a basis.

nodes.name: Dimension is Well-Defined
nodes.statement: All bases of a vector space have the same cardinality.

nodes.name: Trace equals Sum of Eigenvalues
nodes.statement: tr(A) = Σ λᵢ (counted with multiplicity).

nodes.name: Group
nodes.statement: A set with associative binary operation, identity, and inverses.

nodes.name: Ring
nodes.statement: A set with addition (abelian group) and multiplication (monoid) satisfying distributivity.

nodes.name: Field
nodes.statement: A commutative ring where every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.

nodes.name: Ideal
nodes.statement: A subgroup I of (R,+) with rI ⊆ I for all r ∈ R.

nodes.name: Normal Subgroup
nodes.statement: N ◁ G if gNg⁻¹ = N for all g ∈ G.

nodes.name: Group Homomorphism
nodes.statement: f: G → H with f(ab) = f(a)f(b).

nodes.name: Galois Group
nodes.statement: Aut(E/F) is the group of field automorphisms of E fixing F.

nodes.name: Lagrange's Theorem (Groups)
nodes.statement: |H| divides |G| for any subgroup H of finite group G.

nodes.name: First Isomorphism Theorem
nodes.statement: G/ker(f) ≅ im(f) for any group homomorphism f.

nodes.name: Sylow's First Theorem
nodes.statement: If p^k divides |G|, then G has a subgroup of order p^k.

nodes.name: Cauchy's Theorem (Groups)
nodes.statement: If prime p divides |G|, then G has an element of order p.

nodes.name: Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory
nodes.statement: There is an order-reversing bijection between intermediate fields and subgroups of the Galois group.

nodes.name: Second Isomorphism Theorem
nodes.statement: (HN)/N ≅ H/(H∩N) for subgroup H and normal N.

nodes.name: Class Equation
nodes.statement: |G| = |Z(G)| + Σ [G:C_G(gᵢ)] summing over conjugacy class representatives.

nodes.name: Primitive Element Theorem
nodes.statement: Every finite separable extension is simple: E = F(α) for some α.

nodes.name: Totient is Multiplicative
nodes.statement: phi(mn) = phi(m)phi(n) when gcd(m,n) = 1.

nodes.name: Moebius Inversion Formula
nodes.statement: If g(n) = sum_{d|n} f(d) then f(n) = sum_{d|n} mu(n/d)g(d).

nodes.name: FLT for n=4
nodes.statement: x^4 + y^4 = z^4 has no positive integer solutions.

nodes.name: Cyclotomic Polynomial Irreducibility
nodes.statement: The n-th cyclotomic polynomial Phi_n(x) is irreducible over Q.

nodes.name: Gauss's Lemma (Polynomials)
nodes.statement: A primitive polynomial over Z is irreducible over Z iff irreducible over Q.

nodes.name: Hall's Marriage Theorem
nodes.statement: A bipartite graph has a perfect matching iff |N(S)| >= |S| for all S.

nodes.name: Burnside's Lemma
nodes.statement: |X/G| = (1/|G|) sum |Fix(g)|.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Davenport Theorem
nodes.statement: For non-empty A,B subsets of Z/pZ: |A+B| >= min(p, |A|+|B|-1).

nodes.name: Plunnecke-Ruzsa Inequality
nodes.statement: If |A+A| <= K|A| then |nA-mA| <= K^{n+m}|A|.

nodes.name: Young's Inequality
nodes.statement: For p,q > 1 with 1/p + 1/q = 1: ab <= a^p/p + b^q/q.

nodes.name: Vieta's Formulas
nodes.statement: The elementary symmetric polynomials of roots equal (signed) coefficients.

nodes.name: L'Hopital's Rule
nodes.statement: If f/g -> 0/0 or inf/inf and f'/ g' -> L, then f/g -> L.

nodes.name: Alternating Series Test
nodes.statement: If a_n >= 0, a_n decreasing to 0, then sum (-1)^n a_n converges.

nodes.name: Affine Space
nodes.statement: A set with a free transitive action by a vector space.

nodes.name: Eigenvalue
nodes.statement: lambda is an eigenvalue of A if Av = lambda*v for some v != 0.

nodes.name: Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization
nodes.statement: Any linearly independent set can be orthogonalized.

nodes.name: Invertible iff Nonzero Determinant
nodes.statement: A square matrix is invertible iff det(A) != 0.

nodes.name: Orbit-Stabilizer Theorem
nodes.statement: |Orb(x)| * |Stab(x)| = |G| for a group action.

nodes.name: Sylow's Third Theorem
nodes.statement: The number of Sylow p-subgroups divides |G| and is congruent to 1 mod p.

nodes.name: Jacobi Symbol Reciprocity
nodes.statement: For odd a,b: (a/b) = (-1)^(a/2 * b/2) * (b/a) where (a/b) is the Jacobi symbol.

nodes.name: PID Characterization
nodes.statement: R is a PID iff every ideal of R is principal.

nodes.name: UFD Polynomial Ring
nodes.statement: If D is a UFD then D[X] is a UFD.

nodes.name: Rearrangement Inequality
nodes.statement: The sum a_i*b_i is maximized when both sequences are similarly sorted.

nodes.name: Weierstrass M-test
nodes.statement: If |f_n(x)| <= M_n and sum M_n converges, then sum f_n converges uniformly.

nodes.name: Arzela-Ascoli Theorem
nodes.statement: Pointwise bounded + equicontinuous family on compact space has compact closure.

nodes.name: Fatou Lemma
nodes.statement: integral of liminf f_n <= liminf of integral f_n.

nodes.name: Fubini Theorem
nodes.statement: Integral over product measure equals iterated integral when integrable.

nodes.name: Open Mapping Theorem
nodes.statement: A surjective bounded linear map between Banach spaces is an open map.

nodes.name: Closed Graph Theorem
nodes.statement: A linear map between Banach spaces with closed graph is continuous.

nodes.name: Spectral Theorem
nodes.statement: A Hermitian matrix A = U * diag(eigenvalues) * U* for unitary U.

nodes.name: Basis Extension
nodes.statement: Every linearly independent set in a vector space can be extended to a basis.

nodes.name: Row Rank equals Column Rank
nodes.statement: rank(A^T) = rank(A) for any matrix A.

nodes.name: Third Isomorphism Theorem
nodes.statement: (G/N)/(M/N) is isomorphic to G/M when N is normal in M and M is normal in G.

nodes.name: Structure Theorem for Finitely Generated Abelian Groups
nodes.statement: Every finitely generated torsion module over a PID is isomorphic to a direct sum of cyclic modules R/(p^e).

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
nodes.statement: |<x,y>| <= ||x|| * ||y|| in any inner product space.

nodes.name: Eisenstein's Criterion
nodes.statement: If P is prime, leading coeff not in P, lower coeffs in P, constant not in P^2, and f primitive, then f is irreducible.

nodes.name: Angle Sum of Triangle
nodes.statement: The sum of angles in a triangle equals pi.

nodes.name: Thales' Theorem
nodes.statement: An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.

nodes.name: Orthocenter on Altitude
nodes.statement: The orthocenter of a triangle lies on every altitude.

nodes.name: Circumcenter Equidistant
nodes.statement: All vertices of a simplex are equidistant from the circumcenter.

nodes.name: AA Similarity
nodes.statement: Two triangles with two equal angles are similar.

nodes.name: Perpendicular Bisector Equidistant
nodes.statement: A point lies on the perpendicular bisector of PQ iff it is equidistant from P and Q.

nodes.name: Equilateral Triangle Angle
nodes.statement: Each angle of an equilateral triangle equals pi/3.

nodes.name: Exterior Angle Theorem
nodes.statement: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.

nodes.name: Isometry Preserves Distance
nodes.statement: An isometry preserves distances: dist(f(x), f(y)) = dist(x, y).

nodes.name: Isometry Preserves Angle
nodes.statement: An isometry preserves angles: angle(f(p1), f(p2), f(p3)) = angle(p1, p2, p3).

nodes.name: Heron's Formula
nodes.statement: Area = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) where s = (a+b+c)/2.

nodes.name: Orthocenter
nodes.statement: The point where the three altitudes of a triangle meet.

nodes.name: Circumcenter
nodes.statement: The point equidistant from all vertices of a simplex.

nodes.name: Nine-Point Circle
nodes.statement: The circle passing through the midpoints of sides, feet of altitudes, and midpoints of segments from vertices to orthocenter.

nodes.name: Altitude
nodes.statement: The perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side of a simplex.

nodes.name: Incenter
nodes.statement: The center of the inscribed circle of a simplex.

nodes.name: Centroid
nodes.statement: The average (center of mass) of the vertices of a simplex.

nodes.name: Carmichael Function
nodes.statement: The multiplicative order of units in ZMod n is bounded by the Carmichael function.

nodes.name: Units of ZMod
nodes.statement: The number of units in ZMod n equals phi(n).

nodes.name: Squarefree Moebius
nodes.statement: n is squarefree iff mu(n) is nonzero.

nodes.name: Tree
nodes.statement: A connected acyclic graph.

nodes.name: Acyclic Graph
nodes.statement: A graph with no cycles.

nodes.name: Clique
nodes.statement: A set of pairwise adjacent vertices in a graph.

nodes.name: Bipartite Graph
nodes.statement: A graph whose vertices can be partitioned into two sets with edges only between sets.

nodes.name: Connected Component
nodes.statement: A maximal connected subgraph.

nodes.name: Graph Degree
nodes.statement: The number of edges incident to a vertex.

nodes.name: Permutation Sign
nodes.statement: The sign of a permutation: +1 for even, -1 for odd.

nodes.name: Cycle Type
nodes.statement: The multiset of cycle lengths of a permutation.

nodes.name: Descending Factorial
nodes.statement: n^{(k)} = n(n-1)...(n-k+1), the falling factorial.

nodes.name: Multinomial Coefficient
nodes.statement: n! / (k1! * k2! * ... * km!) counts ways to partition n items into groups.

nodes.name: Powerset Cardinality
nodes.statement: |P(S)| = 2^|S| for finite set S.

nodes.name: Product Rule (Counting)
nodes.statement: |A x B| = |A| * |B| for finite sets.

nodes.name: Choose Maximized at Middle
nodes.statement: C(n,k) is maximized when k = floor(n/2).

nodes.name: Polynomial Degree Multiplication
nodes.statement: deg(f*g) = deg(f) + deg(g) for nonzero polynomials over a domain.

nodes.name: Polynomial Derivative
nodes.statement: Formal derivative of a polynomial.

nodes.name: Exponential Addition Law
nodes.statement: exp(a+b) = exp(a) * exp(b).

nodes.name: Log Exp Identity
nodes.statement: exp(log(x)) = x for x > 0.

nodes.name: Exponential Function
nodes.statement: exp(x) = sum x^n/n!, the exponential function.

nodes.name: Logarithm Function
nodes.statement: log(x) is the inverse of exp on positive reals.

nodes.name: Trigonometric Functions
nodes.statement: sin and cos defined via exponential: sin(x) = (e^{ix} - e^{-ix})/2i.

nodes.name: Euler Formula
nodes.statement: e^{ix} = cos(x) + i*sin(x).

nodes.name: Binomial Coefficient Positive
nodes.statement: C(n,k) > 0 when k <= n.

nodes.name: Square Nonnegative
nodes.statement: a^2 >= 0 in any linearly ordered semiring.

nodes.name: Sum Monotonicity
nodes.statement: If f(i) <= g(i) for all i in S, then sum f <= sum g.

nodes.name: Product Monotonicity
nodes.statement: If 0 <= f(i) <= g(i) for all i, then prod f <= prod g.

nodes.name: Noetherian Ring
nodes.statement: A ring where every ideal is finitely generated.

nodes.name: Archimedean Property
nodes.statement: For any x, there exists n in N with n > x.

nodes.name: Well Ordering Principle
nodes.statement: Every nonempty subset of natural numbers has a least element.

nodes.name: Division Ring
nodes.statement: A ring where every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.

nodes.name: Derivative Power Rule
nodes.statement: d/dx (x^n) = n * x^{n-1}.

nodes.name: Integral Linearity
nodes.statement: integral(f + g) = integral(f) + integral(g).

nodes.name: Cauchy Sequence Convergence
nodes.statement: Every Cauchy sequence in a complete metric space converges.

nodes.name: Complete Metric Space
nodes.statement: A metric space where every Cauchy sequence converges.

nodes.name: Uniform Continuity
nodes.statement: f is uniformly continuous if for every eps there exists delta independent of x.

nodes.name: Lipschitz Continuity
nodes.statement: f is K-Lipschitz if d(f(x),f(y)) <= K * d(x,y) for all x,y.

nodes.name: Open Ball is Open
nodes.statement: The open ball B(x,r) is an open set in a metric space.

nodes.name: Composition of Limits
nodes.statement: If f → L and g → M then g(f) → g(L) when g is continuous.

nodes.name: Measurable Set
nodes.statement: A set in the sigma-algebra of a measurable space.

nodes.name: Absolute Convergence implies Convergence
nodes.statement: If sum |a_n| converges then sum a_n converges.

nodes.name: Uniform Limit Theorem
nodes.statement: Uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.

nodes.name: Bounded Continuous Function
nodes.statement: A continuous function with bounded range.

nodes.name: Matrix Transpose
nodes.statement: A^T swaps rows and columns: (A^T)_{ij} = A_{ji}.

nodes.name: Diagonal Matrix
nodes.statement: A matrix with nonzero entries only on the main diagonal.

nodes.name: Determinant of Transpose
nodes.statement: det(A^T) = det(A).

nodes.name: Determinant of Identity
nodes.statement: det(I) = 1.

nodes.name: Trace
nodes.statement: tr(A) = sum of diagonal entries.

nodes.name: Characteristic Polynomial
nodes.statement: det(A - tI), the characteristic polynomial of matrix A.

nodes.name: Minimal Polynomial
nodes.statement: The monic polynomial of least degree annihilating a linear map.

nodes.name: Eigenspace
nodes.statement: ker(A - lambda*I), the eigenspace for eigenvalue lambda.

nodes.name: Linear Independence
nodes.statement: Vectors v1,...,vn are linearly independent if no nontrivial linear combination equals zero.

nodes.name: Span
nodes.statement: The smallest submodule containing a given set.

nodes.name: Direct Sum
nodes.statement: V = U ⊕ W means every v = u + w uniquely.

nodes.name: Dual Space
nodes.statement: V* = Hom(V, k), the space of linear functionals.

nodes.name: Bilinear Form
nodes.statement: A bilinear map B: V x V -> k.

nodes.name: Adjoint
nodes.statement: The adjoint T* satisfying <Tv,w> = <v,T*w>.

nodes.name: Orthogonal Complement
nodes.statement: W^perp = {v : <v,w> = 0 for all w in W}.

nodes.name: Tensor Product
nodes.statement: V ⊗ W, the universal bilinear construction.

nodes.name: Exterior Algebra
nodes.statement: The algebra of alternating multilinear forms.

nodes.name: Finite Dimensional
nodes.statement: A module with a finite spanning set.

nodes.name: Dimension (finrank)
nodes.statement: The cardinality of any basis of a finite-dimensional space.

nodes.name: Quotient Module
nodes.statement: M/N is a module for any submodule N of M.

nodes.name: Quotient Group
nodes.statement: G/N is the group of cosets gN with (gN)(hN) = (gh)N.

nodes.name: Quotient Ring
nodes.statement: R/I is the ring of cosets a+I with (a+I)(b+I) = ab+I.

nodes.name: Kernel of Group Homomorphism
nodes.statement: ker(f) = {g in G : f(g) = e}.

nodes.name: Image of Group Homomorphism
nodes.statement: im(f) = {f(g) : g in G}, a subgroup of H.

nodes.name: Cyclic Group
nodes.statement: A group generated by a single element.

nodes.name: Center of Group
nodes.statement: Z(G) = {g in G : gx = xg for all x in G}.

nodes.name: Simple Group
nodes.statement: A group with no proper nontrivial normal subgroups.

nodes.name: Prime Ideal
nodes.statement: An ideal P where ab in P implies a in P or b in P.

nodes.name: Maximal Ideal
nodes.statement: An ideal M where R/M is a field.

nodes.name: Kernel of Ring Homomorphism
nodes.statement: ker(f) = {r in R : f(r) = 0}, an ideal of R.

nodes.name: Noetherian Module
nodes.statement: A module where every submodule is finitely generated.

nodes.name: Localization
nodes.statement: S^{-1}R, the ring obtained by formally inverting elements of S.

nodes.name: Integral Domain
nodes.statement: A commutative ring with no zero divisors.

nodes.name: Algebraic Extension
nodes.statement: A field extension where every element satisfies a polynomial over the base field.

nodes.name: Separable Extension
nodes.statement: A field extension where every element has a separable minimal polynomial.

nodes.name: Normal Extension
nodes.statement: A field extension where every irreducible polynomial with a root splits completely.

nodes.name: SSS Congruence
nodes.statement: Two triangles are congruent iff all three corresponding sides are equal.

nodes.name: Tangent Perpendicular to Radius
nodes.statement: The tangent to a circle at a point is perpendicular to the radius at that point.

nodes.name: Inscribed Angle Theorem
nodes.statement: An inscribed angle is half the central angle subtending the same arc.

nodes.name: Collinear iff Angle 0 or Pi
nodes.statement: Three points are collinear iff the angle at the middle point is 0 or pi.

nodes.name: Similar Preserves Angles
nodes.statement: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles.

nodes.name: Orthocenter-Circumcenter Relation
nodes.statement: The orthocenter and circumcenter are related by reflection through the nine-point center.

nodes.name: Betweenness Distance Sum
nodes.statement: If B is between A and C then dist(A,B) + dist(B,C) = dist(A,C).

nodes.name: Reflection is Involution
nodes.statement: Reflecting twice returns to the original point.

nodes.name: Affine Independent iff Not Collinear
nodes.statement: Three points are affinely independent iff they are not collinear.

nodes.name: Diameter Distance
nodes.statement: The distance between endpoints of a diameter equals twice the radius.

nodes.name: Sphere/Circle
nodes.statement: The set of points at fixed distance (radius) from a center point.

nodes.name: Midpoint
nodes.statement: The point equidistant from two given points.

nodes.name: Convex Hull
nodes.statement: The smallest convex set containing a given set.

nodes.name: Collinear
nodes.statement: Points that lie on a single line.

nodes.name: Similarity
nodes.statement: A bijection that preserves angles and scales distances uniformly.

nodes.name: Rotation
nodes.statement: A distance-preserving transformation that fixes a center point.

nodes.name: Reflection
nodes.statement: A distance-preserving transformation that mirrors across a hyperplane.

nodes.name: Homothety
nodes.statement: A transformation that scales all distances from a center by a fixed ratio.

nodes.name: Betweenness
nodes.statement: B is between A and C if B lies on the segment AC.

nodes.name: Affine Independence
nodes.statement: Points that do not all lie in a proper affine subspace.

nodes.name: Oriented Angle
nodes.statement: The signed angle between two vectors, valued in the circle group.

nodes.name: Coplanar
nodes.statement: Points that lie in a single plane.

nodes.name: Circumradius
nodes.statement: The radius of the circumscribed circle/sphere of a simplex.

nodes.name: Excenter
nodes.statement: The center of an excircle of a triangle, opposite to a vertex.

nodes.name: Weighted AM-GM Inequality
nodes.statement: The weighted arithmetic mean is at least the weighted geometric mean.

nodes.name: De Moivre Theorem
nodes.statement: cos(a+b) = cos(a)cos(b) - sin(a)sin(b) and the analogous identity for (cos+i*sin)^n.

nodes.name: Dimension of Sum Formula
nodes.statement: dim(U+W) + dim(U∩W) = dim(U) + dim(W) for subspaces U, W.

nodes.name: Trace Invariant under Similarity
nodes.statement: tr(P^{-1}AP) = tr(A) for any invertible P.

nodes.name: Rank of Product Bound
nodes.statement: rank(AB) <= min(rank(A), rank(B)).

nodes.name: Sylow Second Theorem
nodes.statement: All Sylow p-subgroups of a finite group are conjugate.

nodes.name: Nakayama's Lemma
nodes.statement: If M = IM + N with I in the Jacobson radical, then M = N.

nodes.name: Hilbert Nullstellensatz
nodes.statement: I(V(I)) = radical(I) for ideals in polynomial rings over algebraically closed fields.

nodes.name: Going Up Theorem
nodes.statement: For an integral extension R ⊆ S, every prime of R is the contraction of a prime of S.

nodes.name: Krull Intersection Theorem
nodes.statement: In a Noetherian integral domain, the intersection of all powers of a proper ideal is zero.

nodes.name: Krull's Theorem (Maximal Ideal Existence)
nodes.statement: Every nonzero ring has a maximal ideal.

nodes.name: Correspondence Theorem (Groups)
nodes.statement: There is a bijection between subgroups of G/N and subgroups of G containing N.

nodes.name: Determinant Scalar Multiplication
nodes.statement: det(cA) = c^n * det(A) for n×n matrix A.

nodes.name: Trace of Product Commutes
nodes.statement: tr(AB) = tr(BA).

nodes.name: Characteristic Polynomial Degree
nodes.statement: The characteristic polynomial of an n×n matrix has degree n.

nodes.name: Minimal Polynomial Divides Characteristic
nodes.statement: The minimal polynomial of a matrix divides its characteristic polynomial.

nodes.name: Similar Matrices Same Characteristic Polynomial
nodes.statement: If B = P^{-1}AP then charpoly(A) = charpoly(B).

nodes.name: Orthogonal Complement Dimension
nodes.statement: dim(W) + dim(W^perp) = dim(V) for subspace W of inner product space V.

nodes.name: Adjoint of Composition
nodes.statement: (ST)* = T*S* for linear maps S, T.

nodes.name: Positive Definite iff Eigenvalues Positive
nodes.statement: A Hermitian matrix is positive definite iff all eigenvalues are positive.

nodes.name: Change of Basis
nodes.statement: Matrix of composition equals product of matrices: [ST]_B = [S]_B [T]_B.

nodes.name: Eigenvalues of Hermitian are Real
nodes.statement: All eigenvalues of a Hermitian (self-adjoint) matrix are real.

nodes.name: p-Group Has Nontrivial Center
nodes.statement: If G is a p-group then Z(G) is nontrivial.

nodes.name: Index Formula
nodes.statement: |G| = |G/H| * |H| for finite group G and subgroup H.

nodes.name: Maximal Ideal iff Quotient is Field
nodes.statement: I is maximal iff R/I is a field.

nodes.name: Prime Ideal iff Quotient is Domain
nodes.statement: P is prime iff R/P is an integral domain.

nodes.name: Maximal Ideal is Prime
nodes.statement: Every maximal ideal is a prime ideal.

nodes.name: Simple Group Characterization
nodes.statement: G is simple iff it has no proper nontrivial normal subgroups.

nodes.name: Fixed Field of Galois Group
nodes.statement: The fixed field of Gal(E/F) equals F for a Galois extension.

nodes.name: Finite Extension is Algebraic
nodes.statement: Every finite field extension is algebraic.

nodes.name: Localization is Flat
nodes.statement: Localization of a commutative ring at a multiplicative set is a flat module.

nodes.name: Bernoulli Inequality
nodes.statement: (1+x)^n >= 1 + nx for x >= -1 and n >= 1.

nodes.name: Least Upper Bound Property
nodes.statement: Every nonempty bounded-above subset of R has a supremum.

nodes.name: Supremum Bound
nodes.statement: If every element of S is <= b, then sup(S) <= b.

nodes.name: Every Field is Integral Domain
nodes.statement: Every field is an integral domain (no zero divisors).

nodes.name: Characteristic is 0 or Prime
nodes.statement: The characteristic of a ring is either 0 or a prime number.

nodes.name: Exponential is Convex
nodes.statement: The function exp(x) is convex on R.

nodes.name: Logarithm Inequality
nodes.statement: ln(x) <= x - 1 for all x > 0, with equality iff x = 1.

nodes.name: Frobenius Endomorphism is Injective
nodes.statement: The Frobenius map x -> x^p is injective in characteristic p.

nodes.name: Polynomial Derivative Product Rule
nodes.statement: (f * g)' = f' * g + f * g' for polynomials.

nodes.name: Union Bound
nodes.statement: |A ∪ B| ≤ |A| + |B| for finite sets.

nodes.name: Number of Permutations
nodes.statement: |S_n| = n!, the symmetric group on n elements has n! permutations.

nodes.name: Even Number of Odd-Degree Vertices
nodes.statement: In any graph, the number of vertices with odd degree is even.

nodes.name: Double Counting
nodes.statement: Counting edges from both sides of a bipartite graph gives equal sums.

nodes.name: Stars and Bars
nodes.statement: The number of ways to put n identical items into k bins equals C(n+k-1, k-1).

nodes.name: Chromatic Number at most |V|
nodes.statement: chi(G) <= |V(G)| for any graph G.

nodes.name: Bipartite iff No Odd Cycle
nodes.statement: A graph is bipartite iff it contains no odd-length cycle.

nodes.name: Permutation Sign is Multiplicative
nodes.statement: sgn(sigma * tau) = sgn(sigma) * sgn(tau).

nodes.name: Cayley's Theorem
nodes.statement: Every group embeds injectively into a symmetric (permutation) group.

nodes.name: Continuous Image of Compact is Compact
nodes.statement: If S is compact and f is continuous, then f(S) is compact.

nodes.name: Monotone Sequence Converges
nodes.statement: Every bounded monotone sequence of reals converges.

nodes.name: First Isomorphism Theorem (Rings)
nodes.statement: R/ker(f) is isomorphic to im(f) for any surjective ring homomorphism f.

nodes.name: Cauchy Sequence
nodes.statement: A sequence where terms eventually become arbitrarily close to each other.

nodes.name: Subgroup
nodes.statement: A subset of a group closed under the group operation and inverses.

nodes.name: Hahn-Banach Theorem
nodes.statement: Disjoint convex sets (one open) can be separated by a hyperplane.

nodes.name: Uniform Boundedness Principle (Banach-Steinhaus)
nodes.statement: A pointwise bounded family of bounded linear operators is uniformly bounded.

nodes.name: Roots of Unity
nodes.statement: The n-th roots of unity are elements x with x^n = 1.

nodes.name: Convex Function
nodes.statement: f is convex on S if f(tx + (1-t)y) <= tf(x) + (1-t)f(y) for t in [0,1].

nodes.name: Jacobson Radical
nodes.statement: The intersection of all maximal ideals of a ring.

edges.reasoning: The Möbius function is defined directly in terms of prime factorizations: mu(n) = (-1)^k when n is a product of k distinct primes, and 0 when n has a squared prime factor. Without the definition of 'prime number,' one cannot state what 'distinct primes' or 'squared prime factor' mean, making the prime number definition a direct prerequisite for defining the Möbius function.

The definition of prime number is essential to state Dirichlet's theorem: the conclusion 'there are infinitely many primes ≡ a (mod d)' directly references the concept of primality. Without the definition of a prime number, the theorem cannot even be formulated. This mirrors the canonical example of Prime Number being prerequisite to Fermat's Little Theorem.

The definition of prime number is essential to state Wilson's Theorem: the theorem characterizes primality of p ≥ 2 via the congruence (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p). Without the definition of 'prime number,' the statement of Wilson's Theorem cannot be formulated, and primality is central to both the hypothesis and conclusion of the biconditional.

The Legendre symbol (a/p) is defined specifically for an odd prime p, so the definition of a prime number is required to state and define the Legendre symbol. The primality of p is essential both to the definition (distinguishing QR mod p) and to the key properties (multiplicativity, Euler's criterion) that make the symbol well-defined and useful.

The definition of prime number is directly required to state Quadratic Reciprocity: the theorem's hypothesis explicitly refers to 'odd primes p, q', and the Legendre symbol (p/q) is defined only for prime moduli. Without the definition of primality, the statement of QR cannot even be formulated.

The definition of a prime number is required to state and compute Euler's totient function in its most important cases: for a prime p, phi(p) = p-1, and for prime powers phi(p^k) = p^k - p^(k-1). The multiplicative formula for phi(n) decomposes n into prime factors, making the concept of a prime number structurally essential to defining and evaluating the totient function.

The definition of a prime number is essential to state the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: the theorem asserts that every integer > 1 factors uniquely into primes, so without the definition of 'prime' the statement cannot even be formulated. Additionally, primes are the building blocks used throughout the proof. This is a textbook example of a definition being prerequisite to a theorem.

The definition of prime number is required to state the Infinitude of Primes theorem: the theorem asserts that there are infinitely many objects satisfying the definition of primality. Without defining what a prime number is, the statement 'there are infinitely many prime numbers' cannot be formulated. This is confirmed by the Mathlib structure: Nat.Prime is defined in Defs and Nat.exists_infinite_primes imports from Infinite, which depends on Defs.

The definition of prime number is directly required to state Fermat's Little Theorem: the hypothesis 'p is prime' is the central condition of the theorem. Without the precise definition of primality, the statement of FLT cannot be formulated, and primality is essential in the proof (e.g., ZMod p is a field only when p is prime, which drives the argument in Mathlib's FieldTheory.Finite.Basic).

The definition of prime number is essential to state Bertrand's Postulate: the theorem asserts the existence of a prime p in (n, 2n], and 'prime' must be defined to give the statement meaning. Without the definition of Nat.Prime, the theorem Nat.bertrand cannot even be formulated.

The definition of 'Prime Number' is required to state and prove key results in modular arithmetic, such as Fermat's Little Theorem, which directly uses modular congruence. However, the definition of Modular Congruence itself (n divides a - b) only requires the concept of divisibility, not primality specifically. The connection is real but indirect: prime numbers are a central object of study within modular arithmetic, and the definition of prime (via divisibility) shares the same foundational divisibility concept that underlies modular congruence. The link is meaningful but not as tight as a direct prerequisite.

The concept of divisibility from the definition of prime numbers is a prerequisite for defining GCD: gcd(a,b) is defined as the largest natural number *dividing* both a and b, and the notion of 'dividing' is the same divisibility relation central to the prime number definition. More specifically, prime numbers play a key structural role in understanding GCD (e.g., gcd can be computed via prime factorizations), making the prime definition foundational to the full theory of GCD. However, the GCD definition itself only strictly requires the concept of divisibility, not primality per se, so confidence is moderate rather than maximal.

The definition of a prime number is prerequisite to understanding primitive roots mod n, because the most important cases of primitive roots occur when n is prime (or a prime power), and the key theorem that primitive roots exist relies on n being prime. Specifically, the multiplicative group (Z/pZ)* is cyclic of order phi(p) = p-1 precisely because p is prime, making primality essential to the main existence results for primitive roots.

The definition of a prime number is essential to state Euclid's Lemma: the hypothesis 'p is prime' appears directly in the theorem statement, and the defining property of primes (divisibility only by 1 and itself) is what makes the conclusion 'p | a or p | b' hold. Without the definition of primality, the theorem cannot even be formulated. Both share the same Mathlib import (Mathlib.Data.Nat.Prime.Defs), confirming tight structural dependency.

The definition of a prime number is needed to state and prove the key connection between primes and coprimality: if p is prime, then p is coprime to any integer not divisible by p (i.e., gcd(p, a) = 1 when p ∤ a). Without the definition of prime, this relationship cannot be formulated. The concept of prime numbers is a prerequisite for understanding coprimality in the context of primes, though coprimality itself (gcd = 1) can be defined independently of primes.

The definition of p-adic valuation explicitly requires a prime p: v_p(n) is the largest power of *prime* p dividing n. Without the definition of a prime number, the concept of p-adic valuation cannot even be stated, as the parameter p is required to be prime. This is a direct definitional dependency.

The definition of prime number is essential to state the Sum of Two Squares theorem: the hypothesis 'p is an odd prime' is central to the statement 'p = a² + b² iff p ≡ 1 (mod 4)'. Without the definition of primality, the theorem cannot even be formulated. This mirrors the canonical example (Prime Number → Fermat's Little Theorem).

The QR Second Supplement theorem is stated specifically for odd primes p, so the definition of a prime number is required to formulate the hypothesis. The Legendre symbol (2/p) is only defined when p is an odd prime, making the primality definition essential to state and prove B.

The definition of prime number is needed to state and prove the Sum of Totient over Divisors theorem, because Euler's totient function φ(n) is defined in terms of divisors and primality (φ(p) = p-1 for primes, and the multiplicative structure of φ relies on prime factorizations). The proof of Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n typically uses the multiplicativity of φ, which in turn depends on the definition of primality. Without the concept of a prime number, the totient function and its divisor sum identity cannot be properly formulated or proved.

Legendre's Formula computes v_p(n!), where p must be a prime number — the definition of prime is essential to both state and prove the formula, since the p-adic valuation v_p is only defined relative to a prime p. Without the definition of prime number, the formula cannot even be formulated. This matches the canonical 'prerequisite' pattern where A is a definition required to state B.

Lucas' Theorem explicitly requires p to be a prime number in its hypothesis — the modulus in the congruence C(m,n) ≡ Π C(m_i,n_i) (mod p) must be prime for the theorem to hold. The definition of primality is essential both to state the theorem and to carry out its proof (which relies on properties of binomial coefficients modulo a prime). Without the definition of prime number, the theorem cannot even be formulated.

The Euler Product Formula is an infinite product taken over all prime numbers p, so the definition of prime number is essential to even state the theorem. The product Π_p runs over primes, and the formula exploits the unique factorization of integers into primes — which requires knowing what a prime is. Without the definition of prime number, neither the index set nor the factorization argument underlying the proof can be formulated.

The Chevalley-Warning Theorem is stated over F_p, a finite field of prime order, so the definition of a prime number p is essential to state the theorem — the field F_p exists precisely because p is prime. The hypothesis involves a prime p dividing the number of common zeros, making primality a definitional prerequisite for both the setup (existence of F_p) and the conclusion.

The QR First Supplement concerns the Legendre symbol (-1/p) for an odd prime p, so the definition of prime number is required to state the theorem. The condition p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and the exponent (p-1)/2 are only meaningful when p is prime, making primality a direct prerequisite for formulating and proving this result.

The definition of prime number is directly required to state the Lifting the Exponent Lemma: the hypothesis 'p is an odd prime' is the central condition of the theorem, and the concept of primality is essential both in the statement (p | a-b, p ∤ a) and in the proof (primality of p governs the p-adic valuation behavior). Without the definition of prime, the theorem cannot be formulated.

The Freshman's Dream theorem operates in characteristic p, where p must be prime. The definition of prime number is required to state the theorem: 'characteristic p' means the ring has prime characteristic, and the key step in the proof is that the binomial coefficients C(p,k) for 0 < k < p are all divisible by p precisely because p is prime. Without the definition of primality, neither the statement nor the proof can be formulated.

Hensel's Lemma is specifically about lifting simple roots modulo a prime p to the p-adic integers Z_p. The definition of a prime number p is essential to state the theorem — the modulus in 'simple root mod p' must be a prime, and the p-adic structure Z_p is defined relative to a prime p. Without the definition of primality, neither the hypothesis nor the conclusion of Hensel's Lemma can be formulated.

Prime numbers appear fundamentally in the study of binomial coefficients: a classical theorem states that for prime p, p divides C(p,k) for 0 < k < p, which is a key bridge between primality (Number Theory) and binomial coefficients (Combinatorics). This connection is used, for instance, in proving Fermat's Little Theorem via the binomial theorem. The primality definition is essential to characterize exactly when p | C(p,k), making this a recognized structural correspondence between the two domains rather than mere surface similarity.

The standard proof that √2 is irrational uses the concept of prime numbers (or at least irreducibility/primality of 2) as a key ingredient: one assumes √2 = p/q in lowest terms, squares to get 2q² = p², then argues that 2 | p² implies 2 | p (because 2 is prime), leading to a contradiction. The definition of a prime number (specifically that a prime dividing a product divides one of the factors) is essential to this argument, making 'Prime Number' a prerequisite for stating and proving B.

Prime numbers play a distinguished role in polynomial rings: a key bridge is the fact that for a prime p, Z/pZ (a field) yields the polynomial ring (Z/pZ)[X] with special properties (e.g., unique factorization, irreducibility criteria). More directly, primality in number theory corresponds to irreducibility in polynomial rings via the Eisenstein criterion and related results, and the concept of prime elements generalizes from Z to polynomial rings R[X]. The connection is structural: prime numbers generate maximal ideals in Z, and this algebraic structure is foundational to understanding prime/irreducible elements in R[X].

Prime numbers and fields are connected by the canonical theorem that Z/pZ is a field if and only if p is prime. The primality of p (Node A's definition) is precisely the condition that makes every nonzero element of Z/pZ invertible (Node B's defining property). This is a standard, recognized correspondence between number theory and abstract algebra: the definition of prime number characterizes exactly when the quotient ring becomes a field.

Prime numbers play a canonical role in ring theory: an element p in a ring is called 'prime' if p divides ab implies p divides a or p divides b, directly generalizing the number-theoretic definition. The integers Z (the home of prime numbers) are the prototypical example of a ring, and prime elements/irreducibles in rings are the algebraic abstraction of prime numbers. This pair is the standard bridge between number-theoretic primality and the abstract algebraic structure of rings.

Prime numbers canonically give rise to important group-theoretic structures: for any prime p, Z/pZ is a cyclic group of order p, and more generally the multiplicative group (Z/pZ)* is a cyclic group of order p-1. The concept of primality is central to classifying finite cyclic groups (groups of prime order are simple), establishing a recognized formal correspondence between prime numbers and group theory. This is a standard cross-domain bridge where number-theoretic primality directly determines algebraic group structure.

Prime numbers connect to ideals via the standard algebraic correspondence: a prime p ∈ ℤ generates a prime ideal (p) = pℤ in the ring ℤ, and conversely, a nonzero ideal of ℤ is prime if and only if it is generated by a prime number. This is the canonical bridge between the number-theoretic notion of primality and the algebraic notion of prime ideals, routinely used when translating number theory into ring theory (e.g., in Mathlib, Nat.Prime and Ideal.IsPrime are formally linked via this correspondence).

The definition of prime number is directly required to state Cauchy's Theorem: the hypothesis 'prime p divides |G|' explicitly requires knowing what a prime is. Without the definition of primeness, the statement of B cannot even be formulated. This is a clean prerequisite relationship from a definition to a theorem that uses it in its hypothesis.

Sylow's First Theorem explicitly requires the concept of a prime number p in its statement: 'if p^k divides |G|' where p must be prime. The definition of primality is essential to formulate the theorem, as Sylow theory specifically concerns prime-power subgroups. Without the definition of a prime number, the statement of Sylow's First Theorem cannot even be expressed.

Prime numbers connect to Lagrange's Theorem via the structure of cyclic groups of prime order: a group of prime order p (by Lagrange's Theorem) has no proper nontrivial subgroups, making primality the algebraic condition that characterizes these groups. More concretely, Lagrange's Theorem applied to Z/pZ (the additive group of integers mod p, which has prime order) yields that every nonzero element generates the whole group — a key bridge between the number-theoretic definition of prime and group-theoretic structure. This is a recognized correspondence routinely used in introductory group theory.

The concept of a prime number is required in the proof of cyclotomic polynomial irreducibility. The standard proof (via Eisenstein's criterion applied after a substitution, or via the action of Galois conjugates) critically relies on prime numbers: specifically, for prime n, Eisenstein's criterion at prime p|n is invoked directly. Even for composite n, the inductive proof reduces to the prime case. The definition of 'prime' is thus prerequisite to stating and proving the theorem.

The Cauchy-Davenport theorem is specifically stated for Z/pZ where p is prime; the primality of p is essential because Z/pZ is a field only when p is prime, and this field structure is used critically in the proof. The definition of prime number is therefore required to state and prove the theorem. Without the concept of primality, the domain Z/pZ (as a field) and the theorem's hypothesis cannot be formulated.

Sylow's Third Theorem is specifically about Sylow p-subgroups, where p must be a prime number. The definition of a prime number is required to state the theorem: p in 'Sylow p-subgroup' refers to a prime, and the congruence condition '1 mod p' uses p as a prime. Without the definition of primality, the statement of Sylow's Third Theorem cannot be formulated.

The Jacobi symbol (a/b) is defined as a product of Legendre symbols over the prime factors of b, so the concept of prime number is foundational to its definition and to stating the reciprocity law. Without the notion of primeness, the Jacobi symbol cannot be properly constructed, and the theorem's proof relies on reducing to the prime case (Legendre symbol reciprocity). Thus the definition of prime number is a prerequisite for Jacobi Symbol Reciprocity.

The Structure Theorem decomposes finitely generated torsion modules over a PID into cyclic summands R/(p^e), where p ranges over prime elements of R. When R = Z, the prime elements are exactly the prime numbers in the sense of NODE A, and the cyclic components Z/(p^e) are directly indexed by them. This creates a canonical bridge: the number-theoretic notion of prime (NODE A) is the concrete instantiation of the algebraic notion of prime element used in the theorem's decomposition, linking Number Theory to Abstract Algebra via the structure of cyclic modules.

The definition of prime numbers is foundational to the Carmichael function: the Carmichael function λ(n) is defined via the structure of prime factorizations of n, and ZMod n's unit group structure (used in the theorem) depends critically on prime factorizations. Stating and proving bounds on multiplicative orders in ZMod n requires understanding primality, as the key cases are n = p^k for prime p. Without the definition of prime numbers, neither the domain (ZMod n's unit structure) nor the Carmichael function itself can be properly defined.

Eisenstein's Criterion uses a prime ideal P in a ring to test irreducibility of polynomials, bridging Number Theory's concept of primality with algebraic irreducibility in polynomial rings. The prime number definition (Nat.Prime) is the prototypical instance of a prime element/ideal — when one applies Eisenstein over Z, the prime P is literally a prime number. This is a canonical correspondence: the number-theoretic notion of primeness translates into the algebraic structure of prime ideals used in the criterion, connecting Number Theory and Algebra via this shared concept.

The definition of prime number is foundational to the Squarefree Möbius theorem: squarefreeness is defined in terms of prime factorization (no prime squared divides n), and the Möbius function μ(n) is defined via prime factorizations (μ(n) = (-1)^k if n is a product of k distinct primes, 0 if p² | n for some prime p). Without the definition of prime, neither squarefreeness nor μ(n) can be stated, making 'Prime Number' a prerequisite for this theorem.

The definition of prime number is needed to fully understand and state the theorem about units in ZMod n, because when n = p is prime, phi(p) = p-1 and every nonzero element is a unit — the prime case is the canonical special case that motivates and contextualizes the theorem. More directly, the concept of primality is embedded in the structure of ZMod n and its unit group analysis (distinguishing prime from composite n is essential to the proof and statement).
